title: you already speak a little Yiddish
hook: mazel tov, oy vey, schlep: a whole language hiding in English
tomorrow: the plate that tells a story

segments.voice: Yesterday: the candles, two flames before sunset. Your line was light, then rest. Today, words you may have been saying for years.

Mazel tov. Oy vey. Schlep, kvetch, chutzpah, nosh. Plenty of people say these without a second thought, Jewish or not. They aren't slang. They're Yiddish, a whole language with its own songs, newspapers and novels, and a lot of English speakers have been using a little of it all along.
screen: `MAZEL TOV. OY VEY. SCHLEP.` → `NOT SLANG.` → `A WHOLE LANGUAGE.`

segments.voice: Yiddish was the everyday language of Ashkenazi Jews in central and eastern Europe for centuries. It's built mostly from old German, with Hebrew and Slavic words mixed in, and it's written in Hebrew letters. Immigrants carried it to American cities, and English kept a handful. Schlep: to drag. Kvetch: to complain, at length. Nosh: a little snack. Chutzpah: nerve, rude or brave depending on who's telling it. Oy vey is short for oy vey iz mir: oh, woe is me. And mazel tov? Mazel comes from a Hebrew word for a star, and luck; tov means good. Good luck, word for word. But it isn't said before the exam. It's said after the good news: a birth, a wedding, a new job. It means: a good thing happened. Then there's the word worth keeping. In German, Mensch just means a person. In Yiddish, a mensch is a real human being: decent, honest, someone who does the right thing when nobody's checking. The great rabbi Hillel taught it long before Yiddish existed: where nobody is acting like a person should, try to be that person.
screen: `A LANGUAGE IN HEBREW LETTERS.` · `SCHLEP, KVETCH, NOSH.` · `MAZEL TOV — AFTER, NOT BEFORE.` · `A MENSCH — A REAL HUMAN BEING.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. First breath: someone you'd call a mensch. Second breath: one thing they did when nobody was checking. Third breath: let the word land on them, quietly, like a compliment they'll never hear.
Mensch. A real human being: decent, honest, there when it counts. Third word.
Your line: be a mensch. Of everything Yiddish lent to English, that may be the best one. Day three, done.

screen: `DAY 3 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE PLATE THAT TELLS A STORY.`

howItsDone: Yiddish is still spoken in some Hasidic communities and is studied and sung widely; many Jews, religious or not, use Yiddish words every day, say mazel tov after good news, and call a decent person a mensch.

original.note: Yiddish, written in Hebrew letters: a person, and in everyday use, a decent, honorable one.

trapdoor: what you thought: slang words with a Jewish flavor.
what it means: Yiddish, a whole language, and mensch, the kind of person worth being.

what a scholar hears: Yiddish is a Germanic language with Hebrew-Aramaic and Slavic layers, written in Hebrew letters; the mensch proverb echoes Hillel in Avot 2:5: where there are no men, strive to be a man.

story.title: the whole Torah on one foot
story.text: A man walks up to a famous rabbi with a dare: teach me the whole Torah while I stand on one foot. The first rabbi he tries, Shammai, chases him off with a builder's measuring stick. So he goes to Hillel, and Hillel doesn't flinch. What is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor, he says. That's the whole Torah; the rest is commentary. Now go and learn it.

wrong.myth: mazel tov means good luck, so you say it before the big day.
wrong.truth: word for word it's a good star, good luck, but it's said after: congratulations, the good thing happened.

build.prompt: build it: a star, or luck + good.

options: get it back to its owner.
think.reveal: a mensch does the right thing when nobody's checking. that's the whole word.

notes: New lesson 2026-10-06 (research: 'Yiddish words you already use'). The word is mensch rather than mazel tov so the day lands on a value; mazel tov carries the hook and the build, and comes back on day 5 at the wedding.
'For centuries' is used instead of a date for Yiddish's origins (claims rule). Confirm the description: mostly Germanic, with Hebrew-Aramaic and Slavic components, written in Hebrew letters.
Mazel: Hebrew mazal, a constellation or fortune (as in the Talmud's 'ein mazal l'Yisrael', Shabbat 156a); glossed as 'a star, and luck'. Confirm.
Mazel tov said after good news, not as 'good luck' beforehand (b'hatzlacha is used before): common usage; confirm.
Oy vey iz mir glossed as 'oh, woe is me'; confirm.

Hillel's Avot 2:5 line is paraphrased in gender-neutral form ('where nobody is acting like a person should, try to be that person'); the Yiddish proverb 'where there's no mensch, be a mensch' is a popular rendering. Confirm.
Story (Shabbat 31a): the man in the Talmud is a non-Jew asking to convert on that condition; told as 'a man with a dare' for brevity. Confirm.
Yiddish spelling of mensch given as מענטש (YIVO standard); confirm.
